transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi... well, my mom made me come, mostly. Because I just... I can't really make myself do anything anymore. It's like, I wake up, and I just sit there in my room. I'll sit on the edge of the bed or in the chair, and I don't even change my clothes. I think I've been wearing this same sweater and these same sweatpants for... I don't even know how many days now, because it just takes too much out of me to even open the drawer and pick something else out. 

I used to do things, you know? I had this whole basket of yarn, I was knitting this really intricate scarf with cables and everything, and I had my journals—I used to write down every little thing that happened, color-code it with these special pens—and I'd go walking down past the old elementary school every single afternoon. But now... the yarn is just sitting there gathering dust, and the journals are just blank on my desk, and I haven't been outside to walk in forever. I just sit. 

And then my mom will come in, and she'll stand in the doorway, and she asks me, 'What's wrong? Why are you just sitting there?' and I hear her, I really do, but I barely have the energy to even open my mouth to answer her. It's just... everything is just too heavy to even try to form the words to explain it to her, so I just stare at the floor until she leaves. And I guess she just got so worried about me just sitting there in the same clothes every day that she called you.
Have you ever had a period, lasting several days or more, where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or needed much less sleep than usual, even if it felt good at the time?

Energetic? No... no, I don't think I've ever felt like that. I mean, unusually energetic? It's actually the exact opposite, like I was saying about the sweater and the chair. I just feel so heavy all the time. Like my bones are made of lead, or maybe like wet sand, just dragging me down into the mattress. 

The idea of needing less sleep... I mean, sometimes I just lie there in the dark for hours and hours, just watching the way the streetlamp casts shadows on the ceiling, but it's definitely not because I have energy. It's not like I'm wired or wanting to get up and do things. It's just because I'm stuck there. I definitely don't feel good or elated. Even back when I was actually doing things, like when I was knitting that scarf—the one with the cables, I had this really pretty forest green yarn for it, it was supposed to be a gift but I never finished it—even then, I wasn't, like, bouncing off the walls or staying up all night feeling amazing. I just had a normal amount of energy to do regular things. 

But now? Now I can't even imagine feeling elated. I don't even really remember what that would feel like, to wake up and actually want to move my arms and legs, or to feel light. My mom told me the other day that I look like a statue sometimes because I just sit so still for so long, not even blinking much. So... no, definitely not energetic. Never like that. Just... just heavy. Really, really heavy, all the time.
Have you ever experienced a period like this before—weeks or more of feeling this heavy, low, and unable to do things—at some point earlier in your life, before this current episode?

No... no, I don't think so. I mean, I've always been kind of quiet, I guess. Like in high school, I wasn't the one raising my hand all the time or going to all the dances or anything like that. I would mostly just sit in the back row during history class—Mr. Henderson's class, he always had the blinds drawn so it was sort of dim in there anyway—and I would just doodle in the margins of my notebook. But I was still going to class, you know? I was still getting up and putting on my jeans and my sneakers and walking to the bus stop every morning. I wasn't... I wasn't like this. 

I don't remember ever feeling like I literally couldn't move. Like, there were days I didn't *want* to go to school, obviously, because who wants to go to school when it's raining and cold outside? But I still did it. I could still make my legs work. I could still pack my backpack and remember to bring my lunch money. I never had this... this feeling where the air just feels so thick that I can't push through it. 

So, no, I don't think I've ever had weeks like this before. It's just been recently that it got this bad, where I just sit in the chair by the window and watch the dust motes float around in the light for hours, and I can't even bring myself to reach over and turn on the lamp when it gets dark. It's like my whole body just powered down, and I can't find the switch to turn it back on. But before this... no, I was doing things. I was normal. Or, well, my version of normal, anyway. I was definitely moving around.
Have you had any recent illnesses, head injuries, infections, or new medications/substances that started around the same time as these symptoms began?

Illnesses? Head injuries? No, no, nothing like that. I haven't been sick... I mean, I haven't even had a cold or a fever or anything. I haven't even been outside enough to catch anything, really. I just sit in my room, like I said. And I definitely haven't hit my head. I haven't fallen or been in an accident or anything that would cause a head injury. I'm just... sitting. It's hard to get a head injury when you're just sitting in a chair all day, you know? 

And medications... no, I'm not taking anything. My mom keeps asking if I need vitamins, she bought this big plastic bottle of these orange chewable Vitamin C things, and she left them on my nightstand right next to my old alarm clock—the one with the red numbers that are too bright at night—but I haven't even opened the bottle. The seal is still on it. I just look at it sometimes. But no actual medications. No prescriptions or anything new. 

And substances... like drugs or something? No, definitely not. I've never been into any of that. Even in high school, when people would sneak off behind the bleachers during football games—I went to a few games, mostly just because my friend Sarah made me go, but I hated how loud the marching band was—anyway, when people would do that, I never joined in. I didn't want any part of it. I've never even smoked a cigarette or anything. So there's no new substance or pill or sickness that started this. It just... it just happened. Like a fog rolling in, you know? Just slowly covering everything until I couldn't see the point in moving anymore. But nothing physical caused it, as far as I know. Just... nothing.
Have you noticed any changes in your memory, concentration, or ability to think clearly—like feeling confused or having trouble following conversations?

Memory? Um... no, I don't think my memory is any different. I mean, I can still remember things just fine. Like, I remember that my mom bought those orange chewable vitamins last Tuesday, because it was raining and she came in with her umbrella dripping all over the hardwood floor in the hallway. The umbrella has little yellow ducks on it, I've always thought it was kind of childish for her to have, but she likes it. So, no, my memory is perfectly fine. I remember everything I used to. 

And as for concentrating... well, it's not that I can't concentrate. It's just that there's nothing I really *want* to concentrate on. Like, I could probably follow a conversation if I really tried, but mostly people just talk too fast or they talk about things that don't matter. My mom came in yesterday talking about the neighbor's dog—a golden retriever, I think, it's always barking at the mailman—and she just went on and on about how it dug up Mrs. Gable's tulips. And I heard her, I understood all the words she was saying. I just... I didn't care. It just felt like so much effort to nod and pretend to be interested. 

So it's not confusion. I know where I am, I know what day it is... well, usually I know what day it is, unless I've just been sitting in the chair for too long and the days kind of blur together. But that's not because I'm confused, it's just because Tuesday feels exactly the same as Thursday when you don't leave the room, you know? The light comes in the window at the same angle, the dust motes look the same. There's no reason to keep track. But if I really think about it, I can figure it out. My brain still works. It's just... tired, I guess. Or maybe not tired, just... disconnected from everything else. But no, I don't feel confused or anything like that. I can think fine when I have a reason to. I just usually don't have a reason to.
Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, or thoughts that you'd be better off dead?

Hurting myself? No... no, I haven't thought about anything like that. I mean, honestly, doing something to hurt myself sounds like it would take a lot of energy, and I just don't have any. Like, I was saying before about how heavy everything feels? The idea of getting up and, I don't know, finding something to hurt myself with... like we have these heavy orange-handled scissors in the kitchen, in the drawer right next to the stove where my mom keeps the oven mitts and the spare matches... but even just thinking about walking all the way down the hall, past the bathroom, and pulling open that drawer... it's just too much. It's exhausting just picturing it. I don't want to do anything at all, let alone something that takes that much physical effort. 

And as for being dead... I don't really think about that either. I don't think about being dead, but I guess I don't really think about being alive, either. I just sort of... exist. Like those dust motes I mentioned. They aren't alive or dead, they just float there in the sunbeam doing nothing. If I were dead, my mom would probably cry, and she'd have to plan a funeral, and she'd probably invite my Aunt Susan who always wears way too much of this awful perfume—it smells like old roses and baby powder, it's so strong it used to give me a headache whenever she hugged me at Thanksgiving—and it just seems like a huge hassle for everyone involved. 

But mostly, I just don't have the energy to *want* to be dead. Wanting something, anything at all, means you have to actually care enough to want a change. You have to have a spark to want things to be different than they are right now. And I don't. I don't care enough to want to be dead. I just want to sit in my chair by the window. So, no, no thoughts like that. Just... sitting.
How long has this heavy, unable-to-move feeling been going on—do you know roughly when it started?

How long? Um... well, it didn't just happen overnight, like I said with the fog. It was gradual. But if I really try to trace it back to when the fog first started rolling in, when my arms and legs first started feeling like they were filled with wet sand... I guess it was around the time I started that community-college program. 

That was... wow, that was about two years and two months ago. I remember because it was late August, and my mom had just bought me this brand new backpack for it. It was teal. I didn't even want teal, I wanted plain black, but she said teal was more "cheerful" and that I needed to be cheerful for college. She even bought these matching teal notebooks, the ones with the wire spirals that always snag on the sleeves of your sweaters. 

Anyway, I only went to the classes for a little while before everything just started getting too heavy. Getting out of her car, walking across the campus parking lot... they had this huge parking lot with all these deep cracks in the asphalt, and tall weeds growing out of the cracks, mostly dandelions but some of those spiky thistle ones too... and just walking from the car to the brick building started feeling like I was walking through deep water. Every step took so much effort. 

So, yeah, this whole decline, this... this sinking, heavy feeling, it's been going on since then. Two years and two months of just getting heavier and heavier until I ended up just staying in my room, sitting in the chair. It feels like a completely different lifetime, honestly, back when I could actually carry a backpack full of notebooks. Now I don't think I could even lift it off the floor if I tried.

Over these past two years, has the heaviness stayed about the same the whole time, or was there a period where it was milder and you could still function somewhat, followed by a clear worsening into this current state of barely being able to move or care for yourself?

Um... well, it wasn't exactly the same the whole time, no. Like I was saying about the parking lot, at first I could still walk across it, even if it felt like walking through deep water. So it was milder in the beginning, I guess. I could still function somewhat, at least enough to get dressed and sit in those awful classroom desks—the ones where the chair and the table are attached by this thick metal bar, and you have to slide in sideways, and the seat is always made of that freezing cold hard plastic that makes your back ache. I could sit there for a few weeks, taking notes in those teal notebooks. 

But then the heaviness just kept piling on. It got worse and worse, like someone adding more wet sand to my arms and legs every single morning, until I just... I had to stop moving forward in the certificate program. I couldn't do it anymore. The next step was supposed to be this practicum, where you actually go into a real office and do hands-on work. They had this list of places on a bulletin board in the hallway, printed on this bright yellow paper with little pushpins that were missing half their plastic heads. I remember staring at that yellow paper and just feeling the weight completely crush me. I realized I’m just not able to handle the practicum. I couldn't even handle getting out of my mom's car by that point, let alone a practicum where people expect things from you. 

And because I couldn't do the practicum, I couldn't finish, which means I can't plan for the clinic office job I was working toward. That was the whole point of the program, you know? I was going to work in a clinic office, sitting behind one of those glass sliding windows, organizing files and typing things into a computer. I even pictured having one of those ergonomic keyboards that are split down the middle, and a little plastic name tag with my name engraved in white letters. My mom was so excited about it. But I can't plan for that now. The heaviness just completely took over, day by day, until I couldn't even lift my arms to brush my hair, let alone work in a clinic. It just swallowed up the program, the practicum, the job... everything. So, yes, there was definitely a clear worsening. It just slid downhill until all I could do was sit in my chair by the window.
During these past two years, was there ever a stretch of at least two months where you felt completely back to your normal self, with none of this heaviness or low mood at all?

A stretch of two months? Back to normal? No... no, definitely not. I mean, like I was just saying, this whole decline has been going on since I started the community-college program about two years and two months ago. It hasn't stopped or taken a break for even a day, let alone two whole months. 

Two months is a really long time, if you think about it. That's almost an entire season. Like, sitting in my chair by the window, I watch the seasons change. I see the big oak tree out in our front yard—it has these really rough, deep grooves in the bark that look like long, stretched-out faces if the afternoon shadows hit them just right—and I watch it go from having all these bright, almost blindingly green leaves, to turning this rusty, crunchy brown, and then going completely bare with just the gray branches scratching at the sky when the wind blows. Watching all of that happen takes months. And through all of that, through the green leaves and the brown leaves and the snow piling up on the window ledge, the heaviness has just been there. It never lifted. 

I never woke up one morning and thought, 'Oh, I can carry that teal backpack today,' or 'I can go back to normal.' Normal feels like a word that belongs to a completely different person now. Someone who doesn't have wet sand in their veins. So, no, there wasn't any stretch where it went away. There was no break. It's just been one long, continuous sinking feeling since that August two years and two months ago. Every single day, just... heavier and heavier.

Um... I'm not really sure what you mean by that. I haven't noticed anything like that, no. Honestly, it's hard to notice much of anything else when you're just... when you're just stuck in that heavy place I was telling you about. 

When you just sit in the same chair day after day, the world gets really, really small. You don't really experience new things or... or have whatever it is you're asking about. I mostly just sit there and watch the dust float in the air when the sun hits the window at around three in the afternoon. There's this one little crack in the glass, right near the bottom corner of the frame, and the light catches it and makes this tiny little rainbow on the scuffed floorboards... and that's pretty much my whole world right now. Just the dust, and the crack in the glass, and that awful wet sand feeling in my arms. 

Nothing else really gets through. It's like I'm wrapped up in this thick, heavy blanket that just completely blocks everything else out. So... no. I don't have that. I haven't noticed anything like that at all.

Wait, I'm sorry, I think... I think you didn't ask a question just now. You just... you just sort of stopped. Did you ask a question? I'm sorry, my mind is just... it's like wading through mud sometimes, trying to keep up with conversations. 

It's just like how I feel physically, you know? Like my brain is as heavy as my arms. When I sit in that chair by the window—the one with the faded floral pattern where the pink roses look more like gray smudges now because it's so old—I try to listen to the sounds outside, like the cars driving by on the wet pavement, but my thoughts just move so slowly. It's like they're trapped in molasses. So if you asked me something, it might have just slipped right past me, like water through a sieve. 

Could you... could you repeat what you just said? Or ask it again? I really want to answer you properly, I do, but I just need you to say it one more time. I'm trying my best to focus, but it takes so much effort just to keep my eyes open and look at you, let alone process words. It's all just so exhausting. So, um, what were you asking me?

No... no, I really haven't experienced anything like that. Not at all. 

I mean, I sit there in my chair—the one I was just telling you about, with the faded roses—and I spend so much time just staring and existing that I feel like I would definitely notice if something like that was happening to me. But there isn't. My world is just so incredibly small right now. I sit there and trace the worn-out spots on the armrests with my fingers, where the fabric has been rubbed completely thin, just right down to the bare threads from me resting my heavy arms there for over two years. 

There's this one spot on the wall opposite my chair, too, where the paint is peeling... it curls up at the edges and looks kind of like a map of an island, with all these jagged little coastlines. I just stare at that peeling paint for hours, feeling that wet sand in my veins pulling me down deeper into the cushions. When you're trapped like that, wrapped up in that heavy, suffocating blanket I was talking about, nothing else really gets in. You don't have room for anything else to happen. It's just the sinking, the peeling paint, the dust in the light... and that's it. 

So, no, whatever you just asked about, I don't have that. I haven't noticed anything like that at all. It's just the heaviness.

doctor.intent: Establish the presenting complaint that brought the patient to the clinic today
doctor.question: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Mostly I just can't make myself do anything anymore—I sit in my room with the same clothes on, don't knit or journal or go walking like I used to, and when my mom asks what's wrong I barely have the energy to answer.
target_item.reason: This is the first turn of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S023.

patient.answer:
Hi... well, my mom made me come, mostly. Because I just... I can't really make myself do anything anymore. It's like, I wake up, and I just sit there in my room. I'll sit on the edge of the bed or in the chair, and I don't even change my clothes. I think I've been wearing this same sweater and these same sweatpants for... I don't even know how many days now, because it just takes too much out of me to even open the drawer and pick something else out. 

I used to do things, you know? I had this whole basket of yarn, I was knitting this really intricate scarf with cables and everything, and I had my journals—I used to write down every little thing that happened, color-code it with these special pens—and I'd go walking down past the old elementary school every single afternoon. But now... the yarn is just sitting there gathering dust, and the journals are just blank on my desk, and I haven't been outside to walk in forever. I just sit. 

And then my mom will come in, and she'll stand in the doorway, and she asks me, 'What's wrong? Why are you just sitting there?' and I hear her, I really do, but I barely have the energy to even open my mouth to answer her. It's just... everything is just too heavy to even try to form the words to explain it to her, so I just stare at the floor until she leaves. And I guess she just got so worried about me just sitting there in the same clothes every day that she called you.

doctor.intent: Screen for any past history of elevated mood, increased energy, or decreased need for sleep suggestive of a manic or hypomanic episode, to differentiate bipolar disorder from unipolar depression
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period, lasting several days or more, where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or needed much less sleep than usual, even if it felt good at the time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about manic or hypomanic episodes (feeling unusually energetic, elated, needing less sleep), which are symptoms of Bipolar Disorder. My symptom profile does not contain any information about these symptoms.

patient.answer:
Energetic? No... no, I don't think I've ever felt like that. I mean, unusually energetic? It's actually the exact opposite, like I was saying about the sweater and the chair. I just feel so heavy all the time. Like my bones are made of lead, or maybe like wet sand, just dragging me down into the mattress. 

The idea of needing less sleep...
